      11. The spaces : Hölder and Minkowski inequalities#

      Up to now, we measured the size of an integrable function by evaluating . The dominated convergence theorem established conditions under which . For an exponent , the integrals are a family of ways of measuring the size of a function . When the size amplifies values where is large, whereas exponents amplify values where is small. These notes introduce the function spaces of measurable functions for which , and investigate whether the quantity satisfies the properties of a norm, with particular focus on the triangle inequality.

      For , the triangle inequality follows by integrating the pointwise inequality . When , the exponent does not commute with integration, and the pointwise inequality fails for positive numbers. To establish the triangle inequality in this setting, we proceed in three stages.

      First, the concavity of the natural logarithm yields Young’s inequality, which bounds a product of two non-negative numbers by a weighted sum of powers. Second, integrating Young’s inequality after normalizing functions by their respective norms produces Hölder’s inequality, which bounds the integral of a product by for a conjugate exponent satisfying . Third, applying Hölder’s inequality to the components of establishes Minkowski’s inequality, which is the triangle inequality .

      Next, we breifly discuss spaces with exponents , where the triangle inequality fails but a quasinorm inequality holds.

      Finally, we compare the spaces for different exponents on finite and infinite measure spaces. We also interpret Hölder’s inequality as a result of duality of spaces and : are naturally bounded linear functionals on .

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Define as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes and explain why identifying functions that agree almost everywhere is necessary for to satisfy the point-separation axiom of a norm.

      • Determine the exponents for which the power function belongs to and to .

      • Prove Young’s inequality from the concavity of the logarithm, and deduce Hölder’s inequality via homogenization.

      • Prove Minkowski’s inequality and verify that defines a norm on for every .

      • Prove that is a quasinorm on for every , and demonstrate the failure of the triangle inequality when .

      • Prove the inclusion for when , and construct functions showing that this inclusion fails on with Lebesgue measure.

      • Apply Hölder’s inequality to show that each element of defines a bounded linear functional on whose operator norm equals the norm.

      Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space, and functions are measurable functions . On subsets of , the symbol denotes Lebesgue measure.

      11.1 Measuring size with -th powers#

      The integral measures the size of a measurable function . Varying the exponent changes which functions have finite integrals. Power functions on subsets of the real line provide a concrete illustration of this dependence and illustrate the distinct roles of singularities and decay at infinity.

      Example 1 (Power functions near zero and near infinity)#

      For an exponent , the power function is continuous on every compact interval in . Because continuous functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable and the Riemann integral agrees with the Lebesgue integral (Note 23, Theorem 23.1), we compute for and : while for both integrals evaluate to . As , the sequence of functions increases pointwise to , and the sequence increases pointwise to . The monotone convergence theorem therefore implies

      (1)#

      For a fixed parameter , applying the two integrability equivalences in (1) with to the -th power yields This example demonstrates two distinct mechanisms that can cause an integral to diverge. Near , the function is unbounded, so the integrability of requires to prevent excessive concentration of mass on small intervals . Near , the function decays slowly, and the integrability of requires to ensure sufficient decay across the set of infinite measure . These mechanisms correspond to the phenomena of mass concentration and escape of mass to infinity analyzed in the study of integral limit theorems (Note 22).

      11.1.2 Almost-everywhere equivalence#

      In a normed vector space, the norm vanishes if and only if the vector is zero. On the function space , however, the quantity can vanish for functions that are not identically zero. For a non-negative measurable function , the integral vanishes if and only if almost everywhere (Note 21, Proposition 21.1). Applying this property to yields For example, on with Lebesgue measure, the indicator function is non-zero, yet . More generally, if two functions satisfy almost everywhere, then almost everywhere, so . The integral cannot distinguish between functions that differ only on a set of measure zero. To obtain a space on which satisfies the separation axiom of a norm, we identify functions that agree almost everywhere.

An inclusion from smaller to larger exponent spaces holds on measure spaces where positive measures cannot be arbitrarily small, such as with counting measure, where every non-empty set has measure at least .
